    1. invalidatedBy

Annotation Interface Retain

@Documented @Retention(RUNTIME) @Target({TYPE,METHOD}) public @interface Retain
Marks a singleton that survives a restart of the application context in development mode: the instance is not destroyed with the stopped context and is not created again, the next context adopts it. It suits what is expensive to create and independent of the application's classes, such as a connection pool, and is declared by the module that defines the bean, on the bean's class or on the factory method that produces it.

The annotation has no effect outside development mode. In development mode the bean is retained only when it is safe to: its class and everything it received come from the runtime classpath rather than the application's reloadable classes, and it holds nothing bound to the stopped context, such as the context itself, a provider or a lazy proxy. A bean that is not safe to retain is created again, and the log says why.

The decision is read from the bean definition's annotation metadata, without loading the bean's class, by AnnotatedBeanRetentionPolicy.

This annotation is the declarative side of retention, the one a module uses; the mechanism is DefaultBeanContext.stopRetaining(java.util.function.Predicate), which the development launcher, and only it, calls when it stops a context to restart it. That method keeps alive whatever its predicate accepts, but it knows neither which beans are expensive enough to keep nor which configuration change makes a kept bean stale; a module cannot call it, since it does not own the context's lifecycle. The launcher builds the predicate from the retention policies, of which AnnotatedBeanRetentionPolicy accepts the beans annotated with Retain. A policy also names the configuration prefixes that release what it keeps, invalidatedBy() for this annotation, and the context still refuses what is not safe to keep, as described above.

    • invalidatedBy

      String[] invalidatedBy
      The configuration prefixes a change under which releases the retained bean: the next context creates it again from the changed configuration, so that a changed connection URL produces a new pool. A data source would name datasources, for example.
      Returns:
      The configuration prefixes, empty when no configuration change releases the bean
      Default:
      {}
